selected_claim.claim_verbatim: What we want to do is not just export that gas, but we want to have industry and businesses such as data farms, cryptocurrency, others come to Alaska and get five to seven cent kilowatt hour (kWh) gas for 20 or 30 years.
selected_claim.claim_paraphrase_fair: Governor Dunleavy asserts that Alaska's North Slope natural gas can deliver electricity to AI data centers and other energy-intensive industries at five to seven cents per kilowatt-hour for twenty to thirty years, making Alaska a uniquely cost-competitive location for AI infrastructure.
selected_claim.why_smart_people_believe_it: Alaska's North Slope holds enormous proven natural gas reserves, far more than the state currently consumes, and a completed in-state pipeline would theoretically allow those reserves to undercut power prices in data-center markets where Virginia, Texas, and Washington already compete at 6-9 cents/kWh. The Governor is citing an AGDC modeling scenario, not a fabricated number.
selected_claim.steelman: Alaska's North Slope contains vast proven natural gas reserves that are today stranded for lack of a pipeline. If the Alaska LNG Project were built and gas were priced at the wellhead rate plus pipeline tariff, industrial users could plausibly receive power below ten cents per kWh, meaningfully competitive with existing data-center markets. The AGDC has modeled scenarios approaching four to five cents under optimistic pipeline utilization assumptions, which Dunleavy is loosely referencing. Long-term price stability (20-30 years of contracted gas) is a genuine competitive differentiator versus spot-market-exposed Lower 48 grids.
selected_claim.where_it_breaks: The 5-7 cent figure assumes a pipeline that does not exist, has never reached a final investment decision despite decades of attempts, and would cost an estimated $44-60+ billion. Meanwhile, large commercial users on the only Southcentral grid actually capable of powering a data center, Chugach Electric, currently pay 14-17 cents/kWh, and Chugach's own spokesperson has stated the utility currently does not have gas to serve a large data center. The pricing claim confuses a modeled pipeline-era scenario with present deliverable reality.
selected_claim.more_accurate_frame: Alaska's North Slope gas is real and abundant, but it is physically stranded from Southcentral load centers by 800 miles and a pipeline that has not reached a final investment decision. The utilities that would actually power a data center today cannot supply the gas, and the electricity they do deliver costs two to three times the governor's target price. Any investor treating the 5-7 cent figure as a near-term, bankable rate, rather than a speculative post-pipeline scenario, is mispricing the risk.
selected_claim.corrective_thesis: Alaska's five-to-seven-cent data center power pitch is a post-pipeline projection, not a deliverable rate. Southcentral utilities currently charge large commercial users 14-17 cents/kWh and Chugach Electric has stated it lacks the gas supply to serve a large data center at all.

counter_evidence.fact: Chugach Electric spokesperson Julie Hasquet: 'We currently do not have gas to serve a large data center, but we do have generation capacity.' The utility's Cook Inlet gas contract with Hilcorp expires 2028 and Chugach is planning LNG imports, not a new pipeline supply.

ADN opinion (Stan Jones, Apr 12 2026): 'Large commercial users on Chugach's system pay roughly 14 to 17 cents per kilowatt-hour for delivered power,' versus Virginia at 8.99 cents, Texas at 6.12 cents, and Washington at 6.61 cents. Jones concludes: 'Based on what we know today, the answer is no' on whether Southcentral can offer viable electricity pricing for data centers.

Former RCA commissioner Robert Pickett: 'The whole electric industry right now in Southcentral Alaska is in a world of hurt.' Golden Valley Electric (Fairbanks): Cook Inlet natural gas dropped from about 30% of its fuel supply to less than 1% in one year; utility cannot currently support a large data center.

Dermot Cole (Dec 2024): Three data centers each drawing 3 GW would burn 585 billion cubic feet of gas per year, more than eight times the 75 BCF currently consumed across the entire Railbelt for electricity and heating, illustrating that the scale of demand Dunleavy envisions has no existing supply base.

selected_claim.ak_business_consequence: Data center developers, AI infrastructure investors, and DoD/USAF siting offices evaluating Alaska campuses are calibrating capital commitments and site-selection timelines against the 5-7 cent/kWh premise. If that rate is a modeled post-pipeline projection rather than a bankable near-term price, and if the utilities that would actually power those facilities are simultaneously warning they lack gas supply, those investments face stranded-asset risk equivalent to building on a utility promise that the utility itself has not made.
